claims.text: The as-printed alloy has a relatively homogeneous FCC matrix with well-distributed alloying elements.
Before exposure, the alloy has no significant oxide-scale development or grain-boundary embrittlement.
Elevated-temperature degradation is governed by the formation and subsequent instability of protective oxide phases at grain boundaries.
An oxidizing environment produces a transient, continuous Cr-rich and possibly Al-influenced protective oxide scale.
The initially continuous oxide scale slows oxidation.
The protective oxide ultimately becomes discontinuous or spalls because of accumulated stress.
Differential thermal expansion or oxide phase changes generate the stress responsible for scale spallation.
Reducing environments prevent or limit formation of stable protective oxide scales.
The lack of a stable protective scale under reducing conditions permits preferential internal oxidation of Ti and other reactive elements.
Internal oxidation under reducing conditions produces brittle Ti-oxide inclusions concentrated at grain boundaries.
Brittle oxide inclusions cause localized grain-boundary embrittlement.
Grain-boundary oxide inclusions and associated microcracks compromise FCC-matrix cohesion and precipitate catastrophic cracking.
Oxidizing exposure produces an initially slow degradation rate followed by rapid embrittlement and failure after scale spallation.
Reducing exposure produces more uniformly distributed internal oxidation than oxidizing exposure.
Under reducing exposure, Ti-oxide accumulation at grain boundaries causes gradual embrittlement and eventual catastrophic failure.
Catastrophic failure occurs at a lower overall oxidation level in the reducing regime than in the oxidizing regime.
The proposed degradation behavior applies during exposure at approximately 800–1000 °C under oxygen-rich or hydrogen-/CO-rich gases.
Other temperature regimes or inert atmospheres may not activate the same degradation mechanisms.
